extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, economists, commenters, employers, employees, and other stakeholders participating in FTC rulemaking on non-compete clauses
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and synthesis of legal, empirical, and public-comment evidence concerning how non-compete clauses affect competition, new business formation, innovation, market concentration, prices, and product quality. Includes methodological standards the Commission uses to weigh empirical studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions (Section 5 legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 5, an unfair method of competition requires only a tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions; empirical evidence of actual harm is not necessary to establish that conduct is an unfair method of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission may rely on evidence showing a tendency to harm competition rather than requiring proof of realized harm. This legal standard informs the threshold for findings about non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on new business formation (rate of firm entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-competes inhibit new business formation; the Commission finds the weight of empirical evidence establishes that when non-competes become more enforceable, the rate of new business formation (i.e., the number of new businesses formed) declines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in studies as changes in entry rates across state law changes; includes evidence from sector-specific and economy-wide analyses. Consider study weighting and methodological limitations when assessing this metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on jobs created by new businesses (per-firm employment / job creation at startups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-competes reduce the number of jobs new businesses create and decrease average per-firm employment at newly founded firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical measures include reductions in jobs created at newly founded firms (e.g., 7.2% reduction in innovative industries) and decreases in average per-firm employment for spinouts; assess short- and longer-term (e.g., seven-year) outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on innovation (quantity and quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-competes tend to negatively affect innovation, including both the quantity of innovative output and the quality (e.g., value of patents, citations, 'breakthrough' innovations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong studies measure quality (patent value or highly cited patents) as well as quantity, and use multiple legal changes and continuous measures. Consider whether observed patenting reflects true innovation or substitution between protection mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms by which non-competes reduce innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal mechanisms identified: (1) prevent workers from starting businesses; (2) inhibit efficient matching between workers and firms; (3) reduce movement of workers and knowledge flow between firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating innovation effects, explicitly test or account for these mechanisms (founding/spinout rates, match quality, worker mobility and knowledge spillovers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on market concentration, consumer prices, and product quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes are found to increase concentration and consumer prices and reduce product quality, bolstering the finding that they negatively affect competitive conditions in product and service markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these outcomes as both direct harms and corroborating evidence of reduced competition; use direct measures of concentration, price changes, and quality indicators where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of study design features to weight evidence (methodological quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission weights empirical studies based on methodological features such as using several legal changes, continuous measures of enforceability, changes-in-law identification rather than cross-sectional variation, and industry-appropriate controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher weight is given to studies that: (a) use several legal changes, (b) measure enforceability on a continuous/granular basis rather than binary, (c) analyze changes-in-law (difference-in-differences) instead of pure cross-sectional comparisons, and (d) employ appropriate control groups and robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific limitations that reduce study weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that cause the Commission to give less weight to a study include reliance on binary measures of enforceability, examination of only one legal change in one state, cross-sectional-only designs, inability to isolate non-compete changes from concurrent legal changes, and limited outcome measures (e.g., only patent counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using studies with these limitations, interpret results cautiously and consider corroborating evidence from higher-quality studies or qualitative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of timing and measurement of policy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that fail to precisely identify when legal changes occurred (e.g., assume smooth changes over long periods) yield imprecise measures of enforceability and are given less weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer empirical analyses that precisely date policy changes to avoid measurement error in treatment timing and to strengthen causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for concurrent policy/legal changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should isolate the effect of non-compete enforceability from other simultaneous legal or policy changes (e.g., other antitrust law changes) that could confound results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies examining a single state's change must demonstrate that observed effects are not driven by other contemporaneous reforms; otherwise weight is reduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of geographic reallocation versus net national effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether state-level changes simply reallocate innovative activity across state lines or produce a net national change in innovation and business formation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should test for net effects (national-level outcomes) rather than assuming state shifts imply no overall change; evidence that decreasing enforceability in one state increases innovation nationally strengthens causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measurement choices: quality vs quantity (patenting measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing patent counts alone may not capture true innovation; measures of patent quality (value, citations) are preferable to avoid conflating quantity with meaningful innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer metrics like patent value, highly cited patents, or other quality measures; if using counts, discuss possible substitution effects (patenting as a substitute for non-competes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry and worker-group heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of non-competes may differ across industries (high-tech, medical devices, biotech, low-wage sectors) and worker groups (gender, pay level); studies and comments note directional consistency but varying magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess subgroup impacts (industry, occupation, wage level, gender) and report heterogeneity; do not assume uniform effects across all sectors or workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evidence from public comments (litigation threat and chilling effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments describing litigation costs, threats, and chilling effects on entrepreneurship and hiring provide corroborating qualitative evidence that non-competes inhibit startup formation and small-business growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comment excerpts (anecdotes of litigation costs, inability to hire, relocation, lost opportunities) to supplement empirical findings, especially about mechanisms like litigation risk and cost barriers for small firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net impact balancing protective arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of arguments that non-competes protect firms' investments, assets for sale, and encourage entry by protecting small/new firms' investments, but weigh these claims against empirical evidence and availability of less burdensome alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both sides: accept that non-competes may in some instances protect investments productively, but require evidence these benefits outweigh the aggregate inhibitory effects on formation, innovation, and competition; consider viable alternate protections firms can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinouts as a distinct metric and quality consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Spinouts (new businesses formed by splitting off part of an existing firm) are an important outcome; studies examine how enforceability affects spinout rates and spinout quality (e.g., job creation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure both rate and quality of spinouts; note that reductions in spinouts can substantially reduce high-quality firm entry. Control strategies (e.g., using law firms as a control group) affect study weight.
